content_voiceover: Switching to model two, carbohydrate antigens, using ABO as the prototype. Here the blood group gene does not become the antigen itself, it encodes a glycosyltransferase enzyme. That enzyme takes a precursor glycolipid or glycoprotein backbone and attaches a specific sugar onto it, and that added sugar is what the antibody actually recognizes. Looking at the diagram, the backbone starts with fucose attached to build the H antigen, and then A-transferase adds N-acetylgalactosamine, also called galactosamine, to make the A antigen, while B-transferase adds galactose to make the B antigen. So the entire difference between blood type A and blood type B comes down to which single sugar the transferase enzyme attaches, GalNAc for A, galactose for B. This enzymatic, sugar-building logic is the key conceptual difference from model one, where the protein polymorphism was the antigen directly. For boards, remember it's substrate specificity of the transferase, not the antigen structure itself, that the ABO gene actually controls.
keypoints: ABO genes encode glycosyltransferase enzymes, not the antigens directly
A-transferase adds N-acetylgalactosamine (GalNAc) onto the H antigen backbone
B-transferase adds galactose onto the H antigen backbone
H antigen (built by fucosyltransferase) is the shared precursor for both A and B
keypoint_voiceover: For ABO, remember the gene product is an enzyme, not the antigen. A-transferase attaches N-acetylgalactosamine, also called galactosamine, onto the H antigen backbone to build the A antigen. B-transferase attaches galactose instead, to build the B antigen. Both start from the same H antigen precursor, which itself is built by a fucosyltransferase adding fucose. One sugar, added by one enzyme, is the whole difference between A and B.
